newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks surge after market-friendly budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks surge after market-friendly budget.

text.p: Indian stocks zoomed on Friday as euphoric investors went on a buying spree after a market-friendly federal budget.
The benchmark Bombay stocks index surged 178.20 points, or 5.13 percent, to finish at a provisional 3652.99 in a special post-budget trading session.
"Both my markets and I are very happy," said Madan Gopal Damani, the president of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE).

In the 1997/98 (April-March) budget announced earlier in the day, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram cheered capital markets by proposing to withdraw a taxation on income from company dividends, and allowing firms to buy back their own shares.

He diluted a controversial minimum alternate tax (MAT) -- announced in the 1996/97 budget last July -- and raised the investment limit for foreign institutional investors in firms to 30 percent from the current 24 percent.
Chidambaram said MAT would no longer be levied on exporters' profits.
"This is the first time that so much has been done for investors in one budget," BSE's Damani said.
On the National Stock Exchange, the index jumped 63 points, or 6.31 percent, to close at 1061.65. Delhi stocks rose 4.5 percent while shares in Calcutta gained nearly two percent.
"Superb...It was a phenomenal budget," said Sanjeev Mohta, head of research at securities firm James Capel B&K.
"I don't know how he (Chidambaram) managed to do this but it's the best thing that could have happened to the stock markets," he said.
Mohta said 100 leading Indian companies researched by his firm would see their forecast 1997/98 earnings growth jump to an average 26 percent from 19 percent after the new tax cuts.
Chidambaram cut the corporate tax on domestic firms to 35 percent from 40 percent, and on foreign firms to 48 percent from 55 percent.
Capel B&K's Mohta said the biggest beneficiary of the tax cuts would be auto components maker MICO. MICO shares soared 427 rupees, or nearly eight percent, to 5,900 rupees on the BSE.
Chidambaram said India would grant one-time permission to stock brokers to "corporatise" their businesses without attracting tax on capital gains.
"The capital market will gain a lot. Whatever the market has been asking for has been given to it," said R.H. Patil, managing director of the NSE, India's first fully screen-based stock exchange.
